anti_patterns: Anchoring raw data instead of hashes: bloating chain state and leaking private bytes that can never be removed
Treating block wall-clock time as precise: block timestamps drift within consensus tolerance, use block height as the normative binding
Trusting the calendar/aggregator for verification: proofs must verify against independent chain headers, never against the service that sold you the stamp
Timestamping with a broken hash for convenience: preimage resistance is load-bearing, use SHA-256 or stronger
Assuming the anchor proves authorship or ownership: it proves existence-at-or-before-T only, bind identity with a separate signature layer
Discarding proofs or original bytes: without the preimage and the proof bundle the anchor is unverifiable
avoid_when: Sub-second or millisecond timestamp precision is required (block intervals bound granularity)
Data changes frequently and old versions must be forgotten (anchors are permanent)
A single trusted organization can sign timestamps and all verifiers trust it (RFC 3161 TSA is cheaper)
The anchor chain may not survive the required retention horizon
Proof bundles and original bytes cannot be retained for the verification lifetime
benefits: Trustless timestamping: no timestamp authority to trust, verification needs only the artifact, the proof bundle, and independent chain headers
Unbounded batching economics: one OP_RETURN/data output anchors a Merkle root covering thousands of items, amortizing fees to fractions of a cent
Privacy preserving: only hashes leave the client, original bytes never touch the ledger
Self-contained proofs: Chainpoint receipts and OTS proof files verify offline without contacting the anchoring service
Non-repudiable prior art: backdating is impossible once the anchor block is mined, since the commitment cannot predate its own inclusion
Calendar servers are pure convenience: they batch but cannot fabricate inclusion in an already-mined block
best_practices: Hash client-side and submit digests only: the anchoring service must never see artifact bytes
Batch through Merkle trees: aggregate submissions and anchor one root per interval instead of one transaction per item
Treat block height as normative time and block wall-clock as informative projection for human display
Submit to more than one calendar/chain and anchor log roots periodically for redundancy
Retain original bytes plus proof bundles for the full verification lifetime; the chain stores commitments, not your data
Verify against your own node or pinned headers for high-value claims, not a third-party explorer
Plan hash-algorithm agility: record the algorithm in the proof and re-anchor if the hash weakens
component_types: Client Hasher: computes SHA-256 (or stronger) digests of artifacts locally, raw bytes never leave the client
Batch Aggregator / Calendar Server: collects digests, builds a Merkle tree, and publishes the root in a chain transaction (OP_RETURN or data field)
Anchor Writer: issues the on-chain transaction embedding the Merkle root and tracks confirmation/finality
Proof Store: retains self-contained receipts (target hash, Merkle path, anchor reference) alongside original bytes
Independent Verifier: recomputes the digest, replays the Merkle path to the root, and checks root inclusion against its own chain headers
context: Systems that must prove a document, dataset, media file, or log existed at or before a specific time without trusting a centralized timestamp authority: prior-art evidence, audit trails, supply-chain records, ML dataset versioning, and transparency-log checkpoints where any verifier must check the claim independently
design_principles: Existence-only semantics: anchoring proves a byte sequence existed at-or-before-T, never authorship, ownership, or legal status
Verify against the ledger, not the intermediary: aggregators batch for economy but add no trust
Minimal on-chain footprint: commitments on-chain, data and proofs off-chain
Height over wall-clock: consensus-confirmed inclusion order is exact, miner timestamps are approximate
Self-contained verification: proof bundle plus artifact plus headers must suffice with no service call
name: data-timestamping
references: Chainpoint, Chainpoint - Blockchain Proof and Anchoring Standard — https://chainpoint.org/
OpenTimestamps, OpenTimestamps: Stamp and Verify — https://opentimestamps.org
Anchoring Specification v1.3, Anchoring as existence-at-or-before-T primitive — https://anchoring-spec.org/v1.3/
Fassbender et al., Bitcoin-Anchored Temporal Proof for Transparency Services (IETF draft-fassbender-scitt-time-anchor-04) — https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-fassbender-scitt-time-anchor/04/
technology_stack: Chainpoint v2/v3 proofs and verifier libraries
IPFS/Storj for proof and artifact retention
tradeoffs: Coarse time granularity: precision is bounded by block interval (Bitcoin ~10 min, Ethereum ~12 s) plus finality delay
Anchoring latency: calendar batching plus confirmations means minutes to an hour before a proof is independently verifiable
Fee dependence: every anchor batch pays chain fees, which spike with L1 congestion
Retention burden shifts off-chain: the chain holds only the root, so losing the bytes or the proof destroys verifiability
Reorg risk: recent anchors are provisional until buried under enough confirmations
No authorship: existence proofs need a separate signature layer (e.g. BIP-322) to bind identity
use_cases: Prior-art and IP evidence: proving a design or document predates a filing date
Regulatory audit trails: tamper-evident proof that logs existed before inspection
Supply-chain provenance: anchoring batch certificates and handoff records
ML dataset versioning: proving the exact training bytes that produced a model
Transparency-log checkpointing: anchoring Signed Statement or Merkle-root digests per SCITT-style workflows
Media authenticity: proving footage or images predate a contested event
